title: 72-Hour Fall Watch | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: What is a 72-hour fall watch? Learn about the critical monitoring period required after a nursing home resident falls to check for delayed injuries like brain bleeds.
content: After a nursing home fall occurs, the patient should be put on a 72 hour fall watch. This involves a series of thorough assessments to make sure all injuries sustained from the fall are documented and treated appropriately. After the fall, if there are obvious signs of serious injury the nursing home resident should be transferred to an emergency room immediately.
name: 72-Hour Fall Watch

title: 24-Hour Sheets Definition | Nursing Home Records Glossary
description: What are 24-hour sheets? Learn how these documents are used in nursing homes to track resident changes and how they serve as critical evidence in neglect investigations.
content: Twenty-four hour reports are filled out by nurses daily to monitor nursing home (NH) residents and document any changes in residents’ status.
name: 24-Hour Sheets Definition

title: Albumin Levels | Nursing Home Nutrition & Medical Glossary
description: Understand how albumin levels are used to measure a resident’s nutritional status. Learn why low albumin is often a clinical indicator of malnutrition or poor wound healing.
content: Low albumin levels indicates malnutrition. It can also mean that a resident has liver disease or an inflammatory disease. Higher albumin levels may be caused by acute infections, burns, and stress from surgery or a heart attack.
name: Albumin Levels

title: Adult Day Care Abuse | Definition & Legal Rights
description: What is adult day care abuse? Learn the definition of neglect and mistreatment in adult day centers and how to protect seniors who attend these community programs.
content: Adult day care is a planned program of activities in a professional care setting designed for older adults who require supervised care during the day, or those who are isolated and lonely. Adult day care centers enable seniors to socialize and enjoy planned activities in a group setting, while still receiving needed health services. However, elders experience different types of abuse like, physical, sexual, financial, or emotional abuse while at these facilities.
name: Adult Day Care Abuse

title: Definition of Abuse | Nursing Home & Elder Law Glossary
description: Explore the broad legal definition of abuse within nursing homes. Learn how Arizona law classifies various forms of mistreatment and harm directed at vulnerable adults.
content: Arizona state law considers abuse as the intentional physical harm, injuries caused by negligence, unjustified confinement, sexual abuse, and/or sexual assault.
name: Definition of Abuse

title: Braden Score Definition | Nursing Home Neglect Glossary
description: Learn about the Braden Score and how it is used to assess a resident's risk of developing bedsores. Understand why failing to perform this assessment may indicate neglect.
content: The Braden Scale for Predicting Pressure Ulcer Risk, is a tool developed to help health professionals, especially nurses, assess a patient’s risk of developing a pressure ulcer.
name: Braden Score Definition

title: Bed Alarm Definition | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: Learn the definition and purpose of bed alarms in nursing homes. Understand how these devices are used to prevent falls and alert staff when a high-risk resident attempts to move.
content: A type of alarm that can be used for people who have Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, Levy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia or another kind of dementia. Bed alarms are typically used for a couple of different reasons, but the basic idea is that an alarm sounds when someone is trying to get out or does get out of his bed.
name: Bed Alarm Definition

title: Bed Transfer Injuries | Nursing Home Neglect Glossary
description: Define bed transfer injuries and learn how improper lifting or moving techniques by nursing home staff can lead to fractures, drops, and serious resident harm.
content: Elders sustain injuries when they fall attempting to move from one place to another. This includes moving to a chair, wheelchair, bed, toilet or shower chair. It also commonly occurs when, staff need to help residents sit up in bed, move to other areas of a nursing home like the bathroom, get in and out of a bathtub or shower, move back and forth during physical therapy or other medical treatments and move from a bed to a wheelchair for any of the above purposes.
name: Bed Transfer Injuries

title: Bed Sores Definition | Nursing Home Neglect Glossary
description: Learn the medical definition of bed sores (pressure ulcers). Understand how these injuries form and why they are often considered a hallmark sign of nursing home neglect.
content: Bedsores, also known as pressure ulcers, can happen when a person is bedridden or otherwise immobile, unconscious, or unable to sense pain. Bedsores are ulcers that happen on areas of the skin that are under pressure from lying in bed, sitting in a wheelchair, or wearing a cast for a prolonged time. Bedsores are also called pressure injuries, pressure sores, pressure ulcers, or decubitus ulcers. Bedsores can be a serious problem among frail older adults. They can be related to the quality of care the person receives.
name: Bed Sores Definition

title: Coumadin Toxicity | Nursing Home Medication Glossary
description: Understand Coumadin toxicity and the dangers of blood thinner mismanagement. Learn how nursing home medication errors can lead to life-threatening internal bleeding.
content: Warfarin (coumadin) toxicity happens when you have too much warfarin in your body. Certain changes to foods and medicines can also increase the effect of warfarin. Warfarin is a medicine that is used to prevent or treat the formation of blot clots. It works by making your blood clot more slowly. Warfarin toxicity can cause bleeding that can become life-threatening.
name: Coumadin Toxicity

title: C. Diff Infection | Nursing Home Medical Glossary
description: What is a C. diff infection? Learn how this bacterial illness spreads in nursing homes and why proper sanitation is critical to preventing outbreaks among residents.
content: Clostridioides difficile (also known as C. diff) is a bacterium that causes diarrhea and colitis (an inflammation of the colon).
name: C. Diff Infection

title: Elderly Self-Neglect Definition | Elder Law Glossary
description: Learn the definition of elderly self-neglect. Understand the behaviors that signal a senior is unable to care for their own basic needs and when intervention is required.
content: Inability, due to physical or mental impairment or diminished capacity, to perform essential self-care.
name: Elderly Self-Neglect Definition

title: Elder Malnutrition Definition | Nursing Home Glossary
description: Learn the definition of elder malnutrition. Understand the signs of nutritional neglect in nursing homes and how failure to provide adequate food impacts senior health.
content: Malnutrition is often due to one or more of the following factors: inadequate food intake; food choices that lead to dietary deficiencies; and illness that causes increased nutrient requirements, increased nutrient loss, poor nutrient absorption, or a combination of these factors.
name: Elder Malnutrition Definition

title: Elder Abuse Definition | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: Explore the comprehensive definition of elder abuse. Learn about the physical, emotional, and financial harm inflicted on older adults and the laws designed to prevent it.
content: Any knowing, intentional, or negligent act by a caregiver or any other person that causes harm or a serious risk of harm to a vulnerable adult.
name: Elder Abuse Definition

title: Elder Neglect Definition | Nursing Home Abuse Glossary
description: What constitutes elder neglect? Learn the legal and medical definitions of neglect in nursing homes, including failure to provide food, water, and essential medical care.
content: Elder neglect is defined as any failure by a caregiver, whether it is a hired staff or a family member, to fulfill the obligations related to the older person’s care. Forms of neglect typically include any denial of needs related to shelter, food, clothing, hygiene and medical care.
name: Elder Neglect Definition

title: Emotional Abuse Definition | Elder Neglect Glossary
description: Define emotional and psychological abuse in a caregiving context. Learn the signs of non-physical harm, such as humiliation, threats, and isolation directed at seniors.
content: Emotional abuse against the elderly can be verbal or nonverba. Both can be devastating and include the following behaviors: blaming the victim, scapegoating the victim, engaging in demeaning behavior toward the elder, humiliating the victim, ridiculing the victim, ignoring the needs of the elderly person, terrorizing the elderly person, behaving menacingly toward the elder, intimidating the elder, isolating the elder from friends, family or social occasions, yelling at the victim, using threatening behavior against the elder.
name: Emotional Abuse Definition

title: Elder Sexual Abuse | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: Learn the definition of elder sexual abuse. Understand the signs of non-consensual contact in care facilities and the legal protections available to vulnerable seniors.
content: Elder sexual abuse is defined as any act against an elder that is unwanted and sexual in origin. It usually involves those over 60 years of age. Elder sexual abuse includes any sexual contact with an elder who, because of mental illness or dementia, cannot communicate their disapproval of the behavior against them or cannot communicate consent for the activity.
name: Elder Sexual Abuse

title: Feeder Table Definition | Nursing Home Care Glossary
description: What is a feeder table? Discover how these specialized tables are used in nursing homes to assist residents with limited mobility during meals and ensure proper nutrition.
content: A feeder table is used for residents who need assistance and/or supervision with eating. A feeder table typically has a “C” shape to it and seats 4-6 residents. The meal time assistant will be seated on the inside of “C” and the residents will be seated on the outside of the “C”.
name: Feeder Table Definition

title: Gait Belt Definition | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: Learn the definition and importance of a gait belt in a nursing home setting. Find out how this safety device helps caregivers prevent falls during resident transfers and walking.
content: A gait belt is an assistive device which can be used to help safely transfer a person from a bed to a wheelchair, assist with sitting and standing, and help with walking around. It is secured around the waist to allow a caregiver to grasp the belt to assist in lifting or moving a person. When used properly, the belt protects the care recipient from falling and also protects the caregiver from injuring his or her back as they lift or move the care recipient.
name: Gait Belt Definition

title: Group Home Abuse Definition | Residential Care Glossary
description: Understand the definition of group home abuse. Learn about the types of neglect and mistreatment that occur in small residential settings and how to protect vulnerable adults.
content: Group homes, also known as adult foster care or personal care homes, are an alternative to larger assisted care facilities for older adults or people with developmental disabilities. In these homes, elders could experience different types of abuse like, physical, sexual, financial, or emotional abuse.
name: Group Home Abuse Definition

title: Improper Wound Care | Nursing Home Neglect Glossary
description: Define improper wound care in a clinical setting. Learn how failure to clean, dress, or monitor wounds leads to infections and serious complications in nursing homes.
content: If a resident is suffering from a bedsore or pressure ulcer nursing home staff should follow protocol for elder wound care. The patient should be temporarily kept in positions that allow for the least amount of pressure upon the elder wound. Improper wound care occurs when the staff have not followed the protocol.
name: Improper Wound Care

title: Low Air Loss Mattress | Nursing Home Care Glossary
description: What is a low air loss mattress? Learn how this specialized medical equipment helps prevent and treat bedsores by reducing pressure and managing skin moisture.
content: A low air loss mattress has tiny laser made air holes in its top surface which continually blow out air causing the patient to float. This reduces skin interface pressure at the mattress surface. As a result, moisture is moved away and the patient stays dry.
name: Low Air Loss Mattress

title: Medical Director Definition | Nursing Home Leadership Glossary
description: Learn the definition and role of a nursing home medical director. Understand their responsibility for clinical oversight and maintaining the standard of care for all residents.
content: In a healthcare facility, the medical director is responsible for medical supervision and overall regulation of all medical facets that may affect the institutional healthcare system.
name: Medical Director Definition

title: Mechanical Soft Diet | Nursing Home Nutrition Glossary
description: Learn the definition of a mechanical soft diet. Understand how modified food textures help nursing home residents with swallowing difficulties avoid choking and malnutrition.
content: This diet is designed for people who have trouble chewing and swallowing. Chopped, ground and pureed foods are included in this diet, as well as foods that readily break apart without a knife.
name: Mechanical Soft Diet

title: Memory Care Units | Nursing Home & Dementia Care Glossary
description: What is a memory care unit? Learn about specialized facilities designed for residents with Alzheimer’s or dementia and the safety standards required to protect them.
content: Memory Care Units are a form of assisted living facility. The main difference between Memory Care Units and traditional assisted living facilities is that Memory Care Units are specifically for patients who are dealing with dementia and Alzheimer’s.
name: Memory Care Units

title: Nursing Home Administrator Definition | Care Facility Roles
description: Understand the role and legal responsibilities of a nursing home administrator. Learn how leadership oversight impacts resident safety and facility accountability.
content: Nursing home administrators (NHAs) maintain the business and organizational side of long term care facilities. They are also involved on the personal level, focusing on resident care. Above all, the top priorities are quality and safety. To achieve them, NHAs must pair leadership and financial skills with a thorough understanding of the aging process and medical industry.
name: Nursing Home Administrator Definition

title: Nursing Home Understaffing | Definition & Impact on Care
description: Define nursing home understaffing and learn how inadequate personnel levels contribute to resident neglect, medical errors, and preventable injuries in care facilities.
content: Inadequate nursing home staffing causes tragedies, including medical errors, deadly falls and bed sores. A caregiver shortage forces staff to prioritize certain duties over others. This often means overlooking responsibilities like preventing infection, controlling accident hazards, maintaining sanitary conditions and improving resident well-being.
name: Nursing Home Understaffing

title: Nursing Home Abandonment | Elder Law Glossary Definition
description: What is nursing home abandonment? Learn the definition of resident desertion and the legal implications when a caregiver or facility fails to provide necessary supervision.
content: For patient abandonment to occur, the nurse must: a) have first accepted the patient assignment, thus establishing a nurse-patient relationship, and then b) severed that nurse-patient relationship without giving reasonable notice to the appropriate person (e.g., supervisor, patient) so that arrangements can be made for continuation of nursing care by others.
name: Nursing Home Abandonment

title: Nursing Home Abuse Definition | Elder Law Glossary
description: Understand the broad definition of nursing home abuse. Explore the various forms of intentional harm, including physical, emotional, and financial exploitation of residents.
content: Nursing home abuse is any type of harm that comes to elderly residents in long-term care facilities, including physical or emotional injuries, sexual assault, financial exploitation, or other types of abuse.
name: Nursing Home Abuse Definition

title: Osteomyelitis Definition | Nursing Home Injury Glossary
description: Understand osteomyelitis, a serious bone infection that can result from untreated bedsores. Learn about the risks, symptoms, and legal implications of this condition.
content: Osteomyelitis is an infection in a bone. Infections can reach a bone by traveling through the bloodstream or spreading from nearby tissue. Infections can also begin in the bone itself if an injury exposes the bone to germs. Smokers and people with chronic health conditions, such as diabetes or kidney failure, are more at risk of developing osteomyelitis. People who have diabetes may develop osteomyelitis in their feet if they have foot ulcers.
name: Osteomyelitis Definition

title: Physical Abuse Definition | Nursing Home Injury Glossary
description: Understand the definition of physical abuse in a long-term care setting. Learn about the types of intentional force that cause injury, pain, or impairment to seniors.
content: Physical abuse is classified by injuries such as bruising, cuts, and broken bones. Slapping, pushing, and hitting all constitute physical abuse. The improper use of physical or medicinal restraints also falls into the category of physical abuse.
name: Physical Abuse Definition

title: Restraint Injuries Definition | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: Learn the definition of restraint injuries. Understand the physical and psychological risks associated with the use of physical or chemical restraints in nursing homes.
content: Restraints are any type of item that is used to restrain a patient and keep him or her from moving too much, getting agitated, or hurting themselves. In nursing homes, restraints can be both physical and chemical in nature. Injuries or other problems can occur in the forms of strangulation and restricted breathing, bed sores/[pressure sores](https://nursingabuseinjurylaw.com/bedsores-and-nursing-homes/), infections, cuts and bruising, falls, loss of strength and mobility, reduced bone mass, stiffness, incontinence, constipation, frustration, loss of dignity, withdrawal and depression, fear and or, agitation.
name: Restraint Injuries Definition

title: Residential Care Facility Abuse | Nursing Home Glossary
description: What is residential care facility abuse? Explore the definition of mistreatment in RCFs and assisted living environments, and how it differs from hospital-based neglect.
content: Board and care homes, also called residential care facilities or group homes, are small private facilities, usually with 20 or fewer residents. Rooms may be private or shared. Residents receive personal care and meals and have staff available around the clock. Nursing and medical care usually are not provided on site. Abuse as the intentional physical harm, injuries caused by negligence, unjustified confinement, sexual abuse, and/or sexual assault takes place.
name: Residential Care Facility Abuse

title: Residential Treatment Center Abuse Definition | Legal Glossary
description: Learn the definition of residential treatment center abuse. Understand the types of harm that can occur in these facilities and the legal rights of vulnerable residents.
content: A residential treatment center (RTC), sometimes called a rehab center, is a live-in health care facility providing therapy for substance abuse, mental illness, or other behavioral problems.
name: Residential Treatment Center Abuse Definition

title: Shear Definition | Nursing Home Medical Glossary
description: What is shear? Learn how shearing forces contribute to skin breakdown and bedsores in nursing home residents, and how proper handling can prevent these painful injuries.
content: Shear is a mechanical force that acts on an area of skin in a direction parallel to the body’s surface. Shear is affected by the amount of pressure exerted, the coefficient of friction between the materials contacting each other, and the extent to which the body makes contact with the support surface.
name: Shear Definition

title: Significant Weight Loss Definition | Nursing Home Glossary
description: Understand the clinical definition of significant weight loss in a nursing home setting. Learn why sudden weight drops are red flags for malnutrition and neglect.
content: Maintaining good nutritional status is key for preserving the health of a nursing home resident. When good nutrition is not maintained, the resident is at risk for developing bed sores, suffering infection, and having other adverse health events. A significant weight loss is a weight loss of: 5% in one month; 7.5% in 3 months; or 10% in 6 months. Having a resident experience significant weight loss is a “change in condition” which would require physician notification and changes in the care plan, assuming that the loss was unintended.
name: Significant Weight Loss Definition

title: Slide Board Transfer | Nursing Home Care Glossary
description: Discover what a slide board transfer is and how it is used to safely move residents between beds and wheelchairs. Learn about proper usage to prevent nursing home lifting injuries.
content: A sliding board is a piece of equipment that can be used if a person is not able to use their legs to complete a transfer between surfaces or if a standing transfer is not safe to perform. The board is used to make a solid “bridge” between the two surfaces that a person can slide across to transfer between them.
name: Slide Board Transfer

title: Scoop Mattress Cover | Nursing Home Safety Glossary
description: What is a scoop mattress cover? Learn how these raised-edge covers are used as a safety intervention to prevent residents from falling or rolling out of bed.
content: A scoop mattress cover is a convenient way to protect against bed falls. A scoop mattress cover can be used with or without bolsters and assists low risk people by giving them a barrier to prevent them from rolling out of bed.
name: Scoop Mattress Cover

title: Slip and Fall Accidents | Nursing Home Abuse Lawyer Phoenix
content: Slip and falls may result from a wet floor, cracks on the floor, inadequate lighting, improper bed height, improperly maintained wheelchairs, broken steps, or poorly maintained railings.
name: Slip and Fall Accidents

title: Wrongful Death Definition | Nursing Home Law Glossary
description: What is wrongful death? Learn the legal definition of a death caused by the negligence or misconduct of another, specifically within nursing home and elder care settings.
content:
# Wrongful Death in Arizona: Definition, Law, and Nursing Home Abuse Claims

## Why “Wrongful Death” Requires More Than a Short Definition

In many glossaries, wrongful death is described in a single sentence: a death caused by another person’s negligence or wrongdoing. While accurate at a surface level, that explanation does not address the legal rules that determine whether a family can actually bring a claim, who may file it, what damages are allowed, and how deaths in nursing homes are treated [under Arizona law](https://www.azleg.gov/).

Arizona wrongful death law is governed by statute and court decisions that impose specific requirements. Families do not automatically have a claim simply because a death occurred. Legal responsibility must be proven, and only certain family members are allowed to recover compensation.

This page explains wrongful death in Arizona by covering:

-   The legal definition under Arizona statutes
    
-   What must be proven to establish liability
    
-   Who may file a claim and who receives compensation
    
-   How wrongful death applies to [nursing home abuse and neglect](https://nursingabuseinjurylaw.com/)
    
-   Other legal rules that often affect these cases
    

## Legal Definition of Wrongful Death Under Arizona Law

### Statutory Authority: A.R.S. § 12-611

Arizona defines wrongful death under [**Arizona Revised Statutes § 12-611**](https://www.azleg.gov/ars/12/00611.htm). A wrongful death occurs when:

> A person’s death is caused by a wrongful act, neglect, or default, and the injured person would have been entitled to maintain a personal injury action and recover damages if death had not occurred.

This language creates the foundation of every wrongful death case in Arizona.

### Why This Definition Matters

The law does not focus only on the fact that someone died. It focuses on whether the deceased had legal rights before death. If the person could not have filed a [personal injury](https://phxinjurylaw.com/) lawsuit, then a wrongful death claim generally does not exist.

Because of this structure, wrongful death claims are considered legally dependent on the victim’s original injury claim.

 ![Wrongful death in Arizona Nursing Home](https://nursingabuseinjurylaw.com/wp-content/uploads/Wrongful-death-in-Arizona-Nursing-Home-300x200.png)

## What Must Be Proven in an Arizona Wrongful Death Case

To succeed in a wrongful death lawsuit, families must prove the same elements required in a personal injury case:

-   A legal duty of care existed
    
-   That duty was breached by negligence or misconduct
    
-   The breach directly caused the fatal injury
    
-   The deceased had a valid legal claim before death
    

This applies whether the case involves a car accident, medical malpractice, unsafe property, defective products, or nursing home neglect.

Simply showing that a death occurred is not enough. The law requires proof that the defendant’s conduct legally caused the death.

## Who Can File a Wrongful Death Claim in Arizona

### Statutory Beneficiaries: [A.R.S. § 12-612](https://www.azleg.gov/ars/12/00612.htm)

Arizona law limits who may recover damages in wrongful death cases. Eligible beneficiaries include:

-   Surviving spouse
    
-   Surviving children
    
-   Surviving parents or legal guardians
    
-   Personal representative of the estate acting on behalf of eligible family members
    

Relatives such as siblings, grandparents, and extended family members are not automatically entitled to recover compensation unless they also fall into one of the categories above.

### How Compensation Is Distributed

Family Situation

Who Receives Compensation

Spouse or children survive

Paid directly to those individuals

No spouse or children

Parents recover damages

No statutory beneficiaries

Estate may recover

Although the estate may file the lawsuit, the money is legally intended for specific family relationships, not general inheritance purposes.

## What Damages Are Allowed in Arizona Wrongful Death Claims

Arizona wrongful death damages compensate surviving family members for the losses they experience because of the death.

### Economic Damages

These may include:

-   Loss of financial support the deceased would have provided
    
-   Loss of household services
    
-   Medical expenses related to the fatal injury
    
-   Funeral and burial costs
    

### Non-Economic Damages

Arizona also allows compensation for:

-   Loss of companionship and affection
    
-   Loss of care and guidance
    
-   Emotional suffering of surviving family members
    

### Important Legal Limitation

Arizona does **not** allow recovery for the pain and suffering experienced by the deceased before death, even in cases involving severe neglect or abuse.

Estate-based claims may recover certain financial losses, such as medical bills incurred before death, but emotional distress of the victim is not transferred to surviving family members under Arizona wrongful death law.

## When Is a Death Considered “Wrongful”?

Wrongful death claims can arise in many types of incidents, including:

-   Motor vehicle and trucking accidents
    
-   Medical malpractice
    
-   Defective or dangerous products
    
-   Unsafe premises
    
-   Workplace accidents
    
-   Nursing home abuse and neglect
    

In every category, the same legal question applies: did a failure to meet legal duties cause the death?

If the answer is yes and the legal elements are satisfied, a wrongful death claim may be available to the family.

## Wrongful Death and Nursing Home Abuse in Arizona

### Why Nursing Home Cases Are Treated Differently

Nursing home residents are often elderly, physically limited, or cognitively impaired. They depend on caregivers for basic safety, nutrition, medication, and medical monitoring. Because of this dependence, nursing homes owe residents a heightened duty of care.

Arizona law does not treat deaths in nursing homes as unavoidable simply because residents are elderly or ill.

### Common Nursing Home Failures That Lead to Death

-   Dehydration or malnutrition
    
-   Untreated infections and pressure ulcers
    
-   Medication errors or missed treatments
    
-   Falls caused by lack of supervision
    
-   Failure to respond to medical emergencies
    
-   Physical or emotional abuse by staff
    

Many wrongful death cases involve patterns of neglect rather than a single mistake.

### Legal Duties of Nursing Facilities

Facilities are required to:

-   Provide adequate food and hydration
    
-   Monitor medical conditions
    
-   Prevent avoidable injuries and infections
    
-   Respond promptly to emergencies
    
-   Protect residents from abuse and neglect
    

When failure to meet these duties contributes to death, the facility may be legally responsible for wrongful death.

## Arizona Adult Protective Services Act (APSA) and Fatal Neglect

### Statutory Authority: [A.R.S. § 46-451](https://codes.findlaw.com/az/title-46-welfare/az-rev-st-sect-46-451/) et seq.

The **Arizona Adult Protective Services Act (APSA)** protects vulnerable adults from:

-   Abuse
    
-   Neglect
    
-   Exploitation
    

Most nursing home residents qualify as vulnerable adults under this statute.

### How APSA Relates to Wrongful Death

APSA allows legal claims when caregivers or facilities fail to meet basic care standards and that failure results in serious injury or death. These claims may be brought in addition to wrongful death claims, depending on how the harm occurred.

APSA is particularly relevant when neglect occurs over time rather than from a single incident.

### Evidence Often Used in APSA Cases

-   Medical and wound care records
    
-   Staffing schedules and training documentation
    
-   Internal facility incident reports
    
-   Prior inspection and regulatory violations
    

These cases often focus on whether the facility maintained unsafe conditions for extended periods.

## Comparative Fault and Nursing Home Defenses

Arizona follows a **pure comparative fault** system. If the deceased is found partially responsible for the incident, damages are reduced by that percentage but are not eliminated entirely.

In nursing home cases, facilities may attempt to argue that residents caused their own injuries. Courts examine whether proper supervision and care would have prevented the outcome.

## Statute of Limitations for Wrongful Death in Arizona

### Standard Deadline

Most wrongful death lawsuits must be filed within:

-   **Two years from the date of death** under [A.R.S. § 12-542](https://www.azleg.gov/ars/12/00542.htm)
    

### Shorter Deadlines May Apply If:

-   The defendant is a government entity
    
-   The facility is publicly operated
    
-   A notice of claim must be filed within **180 days**
    

Failure to meet these deadlines usually results in permanent loss of the right to bring a claim.

## Why Wrongful Death Law Exists

Wrongful death law serves several important legal purposes:

-   Providing financial support to families after preventable loss
    
-   Holding negligent parties accountable
    
-   Encouraging safer practices and better care standards
    

In nursing home settings, these legal protections play a critical role in safeguarding vulnerable residents who cannot protect themselves.

## Key Points for Glossary Reference

-   Wrongful death is a civil legal claim governed by statute
    
-   Claims depend on the victim’s legal rights before death
    
-   Only specific family members may recover damages
    
-   Both financial and emotional losses may be compensated
    
-   Deceased person’s pain and suffering is not recoverable
    
-   Nursing homes owe residents heightened legal duties
    
-   APSA strengthens claims involving vulnerable adults
    
-   Strict filing deadlines apply
    

## Final Perspective

Under Arizona law, [wrongful death](https://nursingabuseinjurylaw.com/glossary/wrongful-death/) is not simply about loss — it is about legal responsibility for preventable harm. When that harm occurs in nursing homes, where residents rely entirely on caregivers for safety and medical attention, the law provides additional protections through both wrongful death statutes and the Adult Protective Services Act.

Understanding how these laws work together allows families to better protect their rights and hold facilities accountable when standards of care are not met.
name: Wrongful Death Definition

title: Wound Care Nurse Definition | Nursing Home Medical Glossary
description: Understand the role of a wound care nurse. Learn how these specialized professionals are responsible for treating bedsores and preventing infections in care facilities.
content: Wound care nurses provide care for both chronic and acute wounds. An acute wound is a new wound, such as a cut, scrape, bruise or incision that is most often a result of surgery or trauma. A chronic wound is usually caused by a disease or condition, like an ulcer, cancer or diabetes, and may not heal as quickly as an acute wound. WOC nurses are primarily responsible for assessing and prescribing appropriate wound care treatment.
name: Wound Care Nurse Definition

title: Wound VAC Definition | Nursing Home Medical Glossary
description: Learn about Wound VAC (Vacuum-Assisted Closure) systems used in nursing homes to treat complex bedsores and chronic wounds. Understand how this therapy aids in resident recovery.
content: Vacuum-assisted closure of a wound is a type of therapy to help wounds heal. It’s also known as wound VAC. During the treatment, a device decreases air pressure on the wound. This can help the wound heal more quickly.
name: Wound VAC Definition

title: Wandering and Elopement Definition | Nursing Home Glossary
description: Understand the difference between wandering and elopement in a nursing home setting. Learn the legal definitions and the safety risks associated with unsupervised resident movement.
content: Elopement, also known as wandering, in the nursing home setting refers to the patient leaving a facility without notice.
name: Wandering and Elopement Definition
